title: Atomic Structure & Isotopes
description: Subatomic particles, proton and nucleon numbers, electronic configurations of atoms and their ions for elements 1–20, deducing group and period, and isotopes — with the exam traps Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry 0620 sets on each.

notes.heading: The Three Subatomic Particles
notes.body:
0620 marks the particle table almost every year — learn the exact words 'relative charge' and 'relative mass'.

📌 Definitions
• **Proton**: in the nucleus, relative charge +1, relative mass 1.
• **Neutron**: in the nucleus, relative charge 0 (no charge), relative mass 1.
• **Electron**: in shells (energy levels) around the nucleus, relative charge −1, relative mass about 1/1836 — so small it is taken as NEGLIGIBLE (effectively zero).

🔑 How it works
Almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in the tiny central nucleus (protons + neutrons); the electrons contribute essentially nothing to the mass. In a NEUTRAL atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the charges cancel.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying the electron has 'no mass'. The mark scheme wants 'negligible mass' or 'about 1/1836' — an electron does have mass, it is just far too small to affect the mass number.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Proton: +1, mass 1, nucleus. Neutron: 0, mass 1, nucleus. Electron: −1, negligible mass, shells.
• Neutral atom: protons = electrons.

notes.heading: Proton Number and Nucleon Number
notes.body:
📌 Definitions
• **Proton (atomic) number** = the number of protons in the nucleus. This DEFINES the element — every sodium atom has 11 protons.
• **Nucleon (mass) number** = protons + neutrons in the nucleus (protons and neutrons are collectively called nucleons).

🔑 Reading the notation
Cambridge writes an element as $^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$ — nucleon number A on top, proton number Z below, e.g. ²³₁₁Na. For ²³₁₁Na: protons = 11, neutrons = 23 − 11 = 12, electrons = 11 (neutral atom).

💡 Worked Example
³⁹₁₉K: protons = 19, electrons = 19, neutrons = 39 − 19 = 20.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Subtracting the wrong way round. Neutrons = nucleon number − proton number (top minus bottom). For ³⁹₁₉K the answer is 20, not 19 + 39 = 58.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Top number = protons + neutrons; bottom number = protons.
• The proton number is the only count that NEVER changes for an element — ions change electrons, isotopes change neutrons.

notes.heading: Electronic Configurations of Atoms (Z = 1–20)
notes.body:
0620 uses the phrase 'electronic configuration' for the arrangement of electrons in shells — write it as a comma-separated list, e.g. 2,8,1.

🔑 The filling rules (first 20 elements)
• Shell 1 holds a maximum of 2 electrons.
• Shell 2 holds a maximum of 8.
• Shell 3 takes up to 8 (for the first 20 elements).
• Fill each shell completely before starting the next.
For potassium (19) and calcium (20) the third shell stops at 8 and the fourth begins: K is 2,8,8,1 and Ca is 2,8,8,2.

💡 Worked Example
Chlorine, proton number 17, has 17 electrons in a neutral atom: 2 in shell 1, 8 in shell 2, leaving 7 → electronic configuration 2,8,7.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing 2,7,8 or 8,2,7 — the electrons count OUTWARDS from the nucleus, and the shell nearest the nucleus fills first.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• In a neutral atom, total electrons = proton number.
• Check your answer: the digits must add up to the proton number (2 + 8 + 7 = 17 ✓).

notes.heading: Deducing Group and Period
notes.body:
A favourite 0620 deduction question shows you an electronic configuration and asks for the element's position in the Periodic Table.

📌 The two rules
• **Group number** = number of electrons in the OUTER shell.
• **Period number** = number of OCCUPIED shells.

💡 Worked Example
Configuration 2,8,6: outer shell has 6 electrons → Group VI; three shells are occupied → Period 3. The element is sulfur (proton number 2 + 8 + 6 = 16).

🔑 The noble gas check
Noble gases (Group VIII, also called Group 0) have FULL outer shells — 2 for helium, then 2,8 for neon and 2,8,8 for argon. A full outer shell is why they are unreactive, and it is the configuration other atoms are trying to reach when they react.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Swapping the rules — reading 2,8,6 as 'Group III, Period 6'. Group comes from the outer ELECTRONS (the last digit); Period comes from the number of SHELLS (how many digits).

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Last digit → group; count of digits → period.
• Full outer shell → Group VIII noble gas → unreactive.

notes.heading: Electronic Configurations of Ions
notes.body:
This is the single most-lost mark in this topic: the configuration of an ION is not the configuration of its atom.

🔑 How it works
• A metal atom LOSES its whole outer shell: Na (2,8,1) loses 1 electron → Na⁺ is **2,8** — NOT 2,8,1. Mg (2,8,2) loses 2 → Mg²⁺ is 2,8.
• A non-metal atom GAINS electrons to complete its outer shell: Cl (2,8,7) gains 1 → Cl⁻ is 2,8,8. O (2,6) gains 2 → O²⁻ is 2,8.
• The ion always ends with the configuration of the nearest noble gas (a full outer shell).

💡 Worked Example
Ca (2,8,8,2) → Ca²⁺: both outer electrons are lost, so Ca²⁺ is 2,8,8 — the same configuration as argon.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Leaving the lost electron on the ion (writing Na⁺ as 2,8,1) or changing the PROTON count. Only electrons move; the nucleus is untouched, which is why the element stays the same.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Positive ion: electrons = proton number − charge. Negative ion: electrons = proton number + charge.
• Every simple ion in 0620 questions has a noble-gas configuration.

illustration.alt: Shell diagrams showing a sodium atom (2,8,1) losing its outer electron to become Na+ (2,8) and a chlorine atom (2,8,7) gaining one electron to become Cl- (2,8,8).
illustration.caption: Metals lose their whole outer shell — Na⁺ is 2,8, not 2,8,1. Non-metals gain electrons to complete their outer shell — Cl⁻ is 2,8,8.

notes.heading: Isotopes
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Isotopes are atoms of the SAME element that have the same number of protons but DIFFERENT numbers of neutrons. Learn this sentence exactly — it is the standard 2-mark answer.

🔑 What is the same and what is different
• Same: proton number, electron number, electronic configuration — so isotopes have IDENTICAL chemical properties.
• Different: nucleon number, mass — so physical properties (such as density or radioactivity) can differ.
Examples: ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C (carbon has 6 protons; the nucleon numbers differ because ¹⁴C has 8 neutrons, not 6). ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl.

💡 Worked Example
³⁷₁₇Cl: protons = 17, electrons = 17, neutrons = 37 − 17 = 20 — two more neutrons than ³⁵₁₇Cl (18 neutrons).

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying isotopes have different numbers of electrons or different chemical properties. Chemistry is controlled by the outer electrons, and those are identical.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Same protons, different neutrons.
• The mass on the Periodic Table is a weighted average over the isotopes — the calculation is covered in The Mole & Chemical Calculations.

notes.heading: Exam Technique: Deducing Everything from One Symbol
notes.body:
0620 structured questions often give one nuclide symbol and ask for a chain of deductions. Practise the full routine in a fixed order.

🔑 The five-step routine for $^{A}_{Z}\text{X}$
1. Protons = Z (the bottom number).
2. Neutrons = A − Z (top minus bottom).
3. Electrons = Z for a neutral atom; adjust by the charge for an ion.
4. Write the electronic configuration (2,8,8 rule for Z ≤ 20).
5. Read off group (last digit) and period (number of digits) — or noble gas if the outer shell is full.

💡 Worked Example — ³⁷₁₇Cl⁻
Protons = 17; neutrons = 37 − 17 = 20; the ion has charge 1−, so electrons = 17 + 1 = 18; configuration 2,8,8 (full outer shell — the same as argon). The ATOM would be Group VII, Period 3.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting the charge when counting electrons: Cl⁻ has 18 electrons, not 17. And never 'adjust' the proton number — 17 protons is what keeps it chlorine.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Write each particle count down before answering — most slips come from doing it mentally.
• If the question gives an ion, the configuration it wants is the ion's, not the atom's.

flashcards.definition: Subatomic particle in the nucleus with relative charge +1 and relative mass 1. Its number (the proton number) defines the element.
Subatomic particle in the nucleus with no charge (relative charge 0) and relative mass 1.
Subatomic particle in shells around the nucleus with relative charge −1 and negligible relative mass (about 1/1836).
flashcards.example: A neutral chlorine atom has 17 electrons, arranged 2,8,7.

flashcards.definition: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; it defines which element the atom is.
flashcards.example: Oxygen's proton number is 8 — any atom with 8 protons is oxygen.

flashcards.definition: The total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons) in the nucleus; written above the proton number in nuclide notation.
flashcards.example: In ³⁹₁₉K the nucleon number is 39 and the proton number is 19.

flashcards.definition: The arrangement of electrons in shells, written as a comma-separated list filling 2, then 8, then 8 for the first 20 elements.
The group number equals the number of electrons in the outer shell of the atom.
flashcards.example: 2,8,6 has 6 outer electrons, so the element is in Group VI.

flashcards.definition: The period number equals the number of occupied electron shells.
flashcards.example: 2,8,8,2 occupies four shells, so calcium is in Period 4.

flashcards.definition: A full outer electron shell — 2 for helium, 2,8 for neon, 2,8,8 for argon — which makes Group VIII elements unreactive.
flashcards.example: Argon (2,8,8) never needs to gain, lose or share electrons.

flashcards.definition: Metal atoms lose their outer shell; non-metal atoms gain electrons to complete theirs. Every simple ion ends with a noble-gas configuration.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
flashcards.example: ¹²₆C (6 neutrons) and ¹⁴₆C (8 neutrons) are isotopes of carbon.

flashcards.definition: Isotopes have identical chemical properties (same electronic configuration) but can have different physical properties (different masses).
flashcards.example: ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl react identically, but ³⁷Cl atoms are heavier.

questions.stem: Which subatomic particle has a relative charge of −1 and negligible mass?
questions.explanation: The electron has relative charge −1 and relative mass about 1/1836, taken as negligible. A nucleon is any particle in the nucleus (proton or neutron), both of which have mass 1.

questions.stem: In the nuclide symbol ²³₁₁Na, what does the number 23 represent?
choices: The proton number — the number of protons
questions.explanation: The top number is the nucleon (mass) number = protons + neutrons. The bottom number, 11, is the proton number; the neutrons are found by subtraction (23 − 11 = 12).

questions.stem: What is the electronic configuration of a sodium atom (proton number 11)?
questions.explanation: A neutral sodium atom has 11 electrons: 2 fill shell 1, 8 fill shell 2, and 1 starts shell 3 → 2,8,1. The digits must add up to 11.

questions.stem: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of:
questions.explanation: Isotopes differ only in neutron count, which changes the nucleon number but not the element. Same proton number, same electronic configuration, identical chemistry.

questions.stem: How many neutrons are in an atom of ³⁹₁₉K?
questions.explanation: Neutrons = nucleon number − proton number = 39 − 19 = 20. Choice 19 is the proton number; 58 comes from adding instead of subtracting.

questions.stem: What is the electronic configuration of a chlorine atom (proton number 17)?
questions.explanation: 17 electrons fill as 2 + 8 + 7 = 17, so 2,8,7. 2,8,8 is the chloride ION Cl⁻ — the atom is one electron short of a full outer shell.

questions.stem: A sodium atom (2,8,1) forms a sodium ion, Na⁺. What is the electronic configuration of Na⁺?
questions.explanation: The metal atom loses its ENTIRE outer shell: Na loses its single outer electron, leaving 2,8 — the same configuration as neon. Writing 2,8,1 for Na⁺ is the classic lost mark.

questions.stem: An element has the electronic configuration 2,8,6. In which group and period of the Periodic Table is it found?
questions.explanation: Group = outer-shell electrons = 6 → Group VI. Period = number of occupied shells = 3 → Period 3. (The element is sulfur, proton number 16.)

questions.stem: What is the electronic configuration of a chloride ion, Cl⁻ (chlorine has proton number 17)?
questions.explanation: Cl⁻ has 17 + 1 = 18 electrons, filling as 2,8,8 — the argon configuration. 2,8,7 is the chlorine ATOM; the ion has completed its outer shell.

questions.stem: An ion of calcium, ⁴⁰₂₀Ca²⁺, has which number of electrons and which electronic configuration?
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ has 20 − 2 = 18 electrons. The atom (2,8,8,2) loses its whole outer shell, giving 2,8,8 — the same configuration as argon. Only electrons change; the nucleus keeps 20 protons and 20 neutrons.

questions.stem: Why do all isotopes of an element have identical chemical properties?
choices: They have the same mass number
They contain the same number of neutrons
They have the same electronic configuration, and chemical behaviour depends on the outer electrons
questions.explanation: Chemical reactions involve only the outer electrons. Isotopes share proton number and electronic configuration, so they behave identically in reactions; it is their masses (physical properties) that differ.

questions.stem: An ion X³⁺ has the electronic configuration 2,8. What is the proton number of element X?
questions.explanation: The ion has 2 + 8 = 10 electrons. X³⁺ means the atom LOST 3 electrons, so the neutral atom had 10 + 3 = 13 electrons and therefore 13 protons. X is aluminium.

questions.stem: A chloride ion Cl⁻ and an argon atom both contain 18 electrons. Which statement is correct?
choices: They are isotopes of the same element
Cl⁻ has 17 protons but Ar has 18 — having the same number of electrons does not make them the same element
Both particles carry a negative charge
Cl⁻ has the same proton number as argon
questions.explanation: Element identity comes from the proton number, which never changes when an ion forms: Cl⁻ still has 17 protons, argon has 18. They are isoelectronic (same electron count) but different elements, and argon is neutral.

questions.stem: ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl are isotopes. Which statement about them is correct?
choices: ³⁷₁₇Cl has two more electrons than ³⁵₁₇Cl
They have the same proton number and electronic configuration, but ³⁷₁₇Cl has two more neutrons
questions.explanation: Both have 17 protons and 17 electrons (2,8,7), so identical chemistry. The nucleon numbers differ by 2 because ³⁷Cl has 20 neutrons against 18 in ³⁵Cl.

questions.stem: An atom has a nucleon number of 31 and contains 16 neutrons. What is its proton number, and which element is it?
questions.explanation: Proton number = nucleon number − neutrons = 31 − 16 = 15, which is phosphorus. Choice 16 is the neutron count misread as the proton number.
